one_line: Pedro Rodrigues (Supabase) walks through writing agent skills, testing their triggering, and running with/without-skill evals, using a Postgres RLS view bug as the running example.
summary: Pedro Rodrigues from Supabase runs a hands-on workshop on writing agent skills, which he frames as folders of markdown and scripts loaded with progressive disclosure. He argues skills and MCP should be used together: MCP for remote, authenticated integrations and skills for context and workflows. The live demo has an agent build a department-stats SQL view that leaks rows to users who should not see them, because Postgres views bypass row-level security unless security_invoker is set. He then tests a security skill manually and treats skill triggering and behavior as things to measure. The eval method is metrics first, then scenarios with and without the skill, then deterministic assertions plus an optional LLM judge. He shows that his own eval was checking the wrong thing and that LLM graders can be unreliable, so eval code needs the same care as product code. He closes with production advice: keep only the skills in use, version them like docs, and check whether they are actually loaded. Quality is practitioner-level, with some product promotion and auto-caption errors (Anthropic, Supabase, Claude Code are misspelled in captions).

key_ideas.idea: Skills use progressive disclosure: only the name and description (front matter) sit in context, and the agent loads the body or reference files only when the description matches the task.
key_ideas.detail: The SKILL.md acts as an index, reference files act as chapters, and scripts sit alongside. Files can reference other files, so a skill can be a graph. Only SKILL.md with name and description is required. This is the main thing skills add over MCP tool lists.

key_ideas.idea: Skills and MCP are complementary, not rivals. MCP is for integrations and remote tool execution with auth handled by the protocol. Skills carry the context and workflow around the tools.
key_ideas.detail: Scripts in skills run in the local environment and are tied to its OS and dependencies. MCP tools run server-side and need no local setup. Use MCP for an integration and a skill to explain how to use it, including chunking or other usage rules.

key_ideas.idea: Treat a skill as a testable artifact. Define what good means first, write the skill, then run scenarios and grade them, iterating in a cycle similar to TDD.
key_ideas.detail: A skill is free text, so tests have to be eval scenarios with an input, an expected outcome, and the tools that should be called. Grading mixes deterministic checks with an LLM judge. Coming up with good, representative scenarios is the hardest part.

key_ideas.idea: Live demo: the agent built a SQL view over RLS-protected tables and it leaked rows. Views run with the creator's permissions by default, which bypasses row-level security. Setting security_invoker (Postgres 15 and later) makes the policies apply to the view.
key_ideas.detail: The agent reported success because the view existed and returned data, but the test was only checking that the view existed. The fix is a skill that tells the agent to set the flag and to verify access as a different role. The skill also covers keeping RLS enabled on exposed schemas.

key_ideas.idea: Tuning the description changes when a skill loads. Using the verb 'use' followed by the skill's purpose helped it load more often in his tests on Claude. Explicitly naming the skill or invoking it with a slash command is the reliable way to load it.
key_ideas.detail: His claim is that 'use' plus the skill's name almost always loads it in Claude Code. A slash command guarantees loading. Otherwise, test should-load and should-not-load prompts headlessly through the CLI and tune the description against those results.

key_ideas.idea: The eval harness itself can be wrong. In his run, the assertion checked the view directly rather than the relation options, so a correct output was graded as a fail. LLM graders can also hallucinate, so deterministic assertions should come first.
key_ideas.detail: Evals are code, and bad assertions give bad results. He also saw the same prompt pass and fail on different runs, which he attributes to Claude's non-determinism. Reset the database to a known state before every run, because there is no isolated container.

key_ideas.idea: A minimal eval pipeline is an eval.json with prompts and assertions, run in headless Claude Code under two conditions, with and without the skill. Compare the workspace outputs and grading files for each.
key_ideas.detail: He follows the AgentSkills open-standard layout. Assertions can check tool calls or state, or use an LLM judge against a success criterion. The with/without comparison is the core signal. Later, move to sandboxed or Docker runs for a fresh environment.

key_ideas.idea: In production, keep only the skills that are in use, version them with the code, update them when workflows change, and check whether users actually load them.
key_ideas.detail: Skills should sit in CI and be treated as documentation. The CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md should include the skill update workflow. Unused skills are a signal to remove them. Local experimentation can stay messy because descriptions are small.

techniques.name: Progressive-disclosure skill layout
techniques.how: Keep SKILL.md small with a clear name and a description that states when to use it. Move detail into reference files and scripts that the agent loads only when needed. Reference files may link to other files.
techniques.when: When domain knowledge is large and you do not want it all in context on every turn, or when you have many skills installed.

techniques.name: Trigger-accuracy testing via headless CLI
techniques.how: Write a set of prompts where the skill should load and a set where it should not. Run them headlessly in the agent CLI, log whether the skill was loaded, and adjust the description until the results match. Start the description with 'use' followed by the purpose.
techniques.when: Before relying on a skill to auto-load, or after changing its description.

techniques.name: With/without skill eval comparison
techniques.how: Define scenarios in eval.json with a prompt and assertions. Run each scenario twice in headless mode, once with the skill injected and once without. Compare grading output and the resulting artifacts for both runs.
techniques.when: To measure whether a skill actually changes agent behavior, and to catch regressions when the skill changes.

techniques.name: Deterministic state assertions before LLM judging
techniques.how: Check the real system state with code, such as querying catalog or relation options, rather than only inspecting an output snippet. Use an LLM judge only for the parts code cannot check. Reset the database to a seeded state before each run.
techniques.when: Any eval that touches a database or external system, where non-determinism or false failures would otherwise mislead you.

techniques.name: MCP tool plus skill split for data access
techniques.how: Expose data access as an MCP tool with parameters such as chunk or buffer size, which handles auth and remote execution. Put the usage rules in a skill, such as how to load large schemas in chunks.
techniques.when: When an agent must query large or remote schemas and you want to avoid loading everything into context.

techniques.name: security_invoker for Postgres views over RLS tables
techniques.how: On Postgres 15 or later, create views with security_invoker so that the querying user's RLS policies apply. Then verify by querying the view as a restricted role, not only by checking that the view exists.
techniques.when: Any time an agent or developer creates a view over a table that has row-level security enabled.

techniques.name: Skill install via npm skills package with symlinks
techniques.how: Use the Vercel skills npm package to install from a local path or a repo. It places the skill in an .agents folder and symlinks it into .claude/skills so both locations resolve.
techniques.when: When you want to share or install skills across projects and agent harnesses without copying files by hand.

numbers.claim: Loading a skill's full SKILL.md used about 1.3k tokens of context in his session, and he says that is much less than loading the equivalent MCP tool set.
The Supabase MCP server exposes about 29 tools in the full local version and about 20 in the smaller production version.
The demo performance-review app has 4 employees across roles (one employee, two managers, one HR).
Mentioning 'use' plus the skill name, or using a slash command, loads the skill almost 100% of the time, per his experience.
Postgres 15 or later supports the security_invoker flag on views, which applies the querying user's RLS policies to the view.
The workshop lasted 1h18m and ran two conditions (with and without skill) for the eval.

hot_takes: You should use both MCP and skills, not one or the other.
Skill descriptions matter more than skill bodies, because the description decides whether the skill loads at all.
Evals are just code, so a wrong assertion can make a working system look broken.
An LLM judge can hallucinate, so deterministic checks should come before LLM grading.
Skills in production should be treated as documentation that gets updated with the code.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI and has a skill-ranking feature. The talk's headless with/without-skill eval and should-load/should-not-load trigger tests map directly onto that.
relevance.action: Add a headless with/without-skill eval and a should-load/should-not-load trigger test set for skill ranking, then compare the results across skill descriptions.

relevance.why: AgentOS uses Postgres and plans SkillForge, which needs a skill-worthiness signal. The talk's 'is this skill loaded by users' signal and its RLS-view bug are both relevant.
relevance.action: Audit any Postgres views over RLS-protected tenant tables and set security_invoker, adding a test that queries the view as a restricted role. Also record skill-load rate as a candidate signal for SkillForge skill-worthiness scoring.

relevance.why: The talk gives a concrete eval method for any agent instruction file (CLAUDE.md, skills), including the with/without comparison and the warning that eval code can be wrong.
relevance.action: Before shipping a new skill or CLAUDE.md rule, write 5 to 10 eval scenarios with deterministic assertions and run them with and without the rule.
